title: MG MGS6 EV Essence RWD from $48,990 Driveaway @ MG
body:
Deal: MG MGS6 EV Essence RWD from $48,990 Driveaway @ MG

[Sortale] not throwing shade, just trying to help because I was considering this car
the battery is NCM (Nickel Cobalt Manganese) vs LFP (Lithium Iron Phosphate) as is used by BYD or Tesla
LFP is suposed to be more stable and can hold high level charge (>80%) with less degradation than NCM
I assume that is why the MGS6 is cheaper than the other despite the better number on paper
[maverickjohn] My Tesla Model Y L is a NMC battery.
I'm pretty sure only base trim have LFP and that's because they take up more space meaning less mileage.
NMC all can travel further. It just means for day to day use you need to charge to 80% when you plan a long drive it's definitely fine to charge to 100%
[urbancartel] From what? Maybe put that in the title or description
[zappy] When I was looking last month it used to be $49,990 drive away.
[xyron] Plenty of sub-2000km demos floating around dealers for the low $40s. have been tempted by one but the lack of OTA updates gives me the ipps
[fantombloo] the lack of OTA updates
I've now read this as a drawback a few times in various comments. IDK but being untethered actually makes me more comfortable. Critical updates can be done at service. If / when sh!t hits the fan the car will still drive without remote interruptions.
[1tightwad] FBT exemptions for EVs on lease drives a lot of if
[dkausa] For those in a house with solar and battery, and free energy available between 11am-2pm (or even an 8c/kwh EV plan), they make a lot of sense.
Decent used EVs are at reasonable prices. Used 2023 MG4s go for around the $20K mark with 7 years of manufacturers warranty remaining (less than a used hybrid Corolla). Higher depreciation will be argued, but it's already depreciated, so it's at the used buyer's advantage.
If you drive 15,000KMs a year in a car that does 6.0L/100KM, with a fuel price of $2.20/L, then that's about $2000 a year. Plus oil changes/timing belts/trans fluid/spark plugs at some stage.
EV on the 8c/kwh plan, that's $216 a year (or $0 on solar/free power). It does have coolant that needs changing eventually.
Certainly get that for those who cannot charge at home, it is not so simple.
[muwu] My fuel cost averaging ~4.0L/100km and my replacement hybrid battery cost will be ~$2,000-5,000. This is much less than the depreciation on an EV, and far less than a full EV battery replacement if you try to keep it long-term. The math is clear
[Flurogreen] @muwu: That math isnt "clear". Modern EV batteries are likely to last the life of the vehicle. https://www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/electric-vehicle… EVs are doing alot better in the second hand market than ICE vehicles right no, there is just a lot less of them, especially post 2022 ones. Hybrid are the worst of both worlds, you have an engine to maintain as well as an EV drivetrain, more complexity and higher emissions.
[muwu] @Flurogreen: The "life of the vehicle" is important to define.
Lithium batteries powering motor vehicle engines do last an average 10-15 years (with some individual variability).
For a first owner, it's reselling before they need to front up the cost of a full EV battery replacement (typical ownership might be between 3 to 9 years) and the depreciation is steep, appropriately so.
For a used car owner, the life is actually truer to what's practical, that is fronting up the cost of a battery replacement and maintaining a used vehicle for ~15-30 years. Here you are saved from the steep depreciation but need to justify the high full EV battery replacement cost as you're intending to own long-term.
The second owner of an EV isn't too different from a hybrid buyer. They are both owning vehicles where the depreciation curve is leveling off and have more evened out costs of keeping their car on the road year-to-year.
Yes, maintenance of a hybrid with its ICE is higher (this cost can only be managed by buying a reliable Japanese model with lower mass market parts and labour).
But depreciation (and in the case of EV, the inverse of this math being battery replacement), is always a lot more than maintenance and fuelling (it's why every car owner who understand the economics of their purchase pays heed to depreciation above all else).
The secondhand market is a clear signal to where to value lies - depreciation of hybrid is small, depreciation of EVs is large (this tell you 90% of the story, the rest of the 100% is told through doing the rest of the math).
[muwu] I looked at the salary packinging arithmetic (as a healthcare worker) - I can see the incentives on tax, but the depreciation on a new EV just blows the math out of the water. I went for a used hybrid with post-tax cash, and the math on the comparison is inarguably better
[Matt P] Nothing stopping anyone salary packaging a used EV. Those 20k MG4s can be leased.
Then further claims can be made for "reimbursement" from pre-tax dollars on home charging costs.
[muwu] @Matt P: Yep.
One, the used EV is still on a steeper depreciation curve than the used hybrid (admittingly less than the new EV).
Two, getting a leasing company to do their package on a used vehicle comes with quite a few headaches (they want you to buy a new EV). Of course, it can be done, for sure, but the rates and the contract they try on you is painful to negotiate your way through and you're better going direct to a banking lender for your loan than relying on a packaging company alone (I've seen this first-hand with a fellow healthcare worker who did a much better deal with a bank directly to get the loan on a simpler and lower rate, but he will still lose out on the depreciation of his EV).
[Matt P] @muwu: The difference of a few percent on a loan is miniscule compared to the 35ish cents per dollar you're likely dodging in tax. If you're in healthcare, max out your workplace/benevolent instution FBT exemption on mortgage payments/rent and utilise the FBT exemption on EVs separately.
If the offering from the NL company is garbage, take that to your People & Culture/Finance/whoever owns staff benefits and protest. Speak to other providers who will offer a better deal. Put their offering to the business as a better option.
[muwu] @Matt P: I've done the analysis. Novate leasing an EV can certainly maximise tax savings, but the lease fees and depreciation is much greater.
I judge the economics of any capital input based on post-tax gain/cost, not tax alone. Paying for a vehicle outright post-tax, is superior to a lease (and this is coming from an income earner on a 47% marginal income tax rate, I squeezed these numbers as hard as I could in my analysis to try to justify the salary packaging and therefore reduce my tax bill to the ATO, believe me on that!). I could only justify the new EV (or even a few years old) on a lease if I REALLY wanted the EV instead of the hybrid, and this is exactly where my colleagues find themselves and ultimately paying more (to be fair, they haven't analysed the numbers as hard as I have, and they're happy to get on with their lives with the decision they've made, all power to them).
[nickelanddime] EVs (mostly Chinese ones) are more affordable than equivalent ICE vehicles. Most EVs have a minimum 7-8 year warranty on their battery which is probably as long as the average Australian keeps their car anyway. No one is replacing their battery since it’s pretty much the majority of the value of the car, better off just buying another cheap EV if it comes to it 15 years down the road.
If you plan on keeping your car for a long time, depreciation is moot considering the savings in fuel, servicing and repairs (multiple thousands of dollars a year).
I don’t know what else EVs can do to prove they are superior financially.
[muwu] You've defined the math perfectly.
No one is replacing the EV full battery cost, hence it's steep depreciation (one of the main factors). That's why the hybrids, with there much more modest battery replacement costs and much of the fuelling and some of the maintenance savings, are the mathetically superior choice (right now, it will change).
Depreciation on a hybrid is not moot, because that annualised loss is less cf. EV whenever I decide to sell, and the running cost if you're intending to hold long-term and therefore amortise the battery replacement cost, does end up cheaper.
I do wish the math was superior for EV over hybrid, because I want to be driving a full EV over a hybrid, I am sold by the tech, but the economics just don't quite make sense just yet. They will, and I'm excited by my next purchase being an EV 👍
[Fernet] Is there an assumption depreciation will be the same for one type of vehicle over another in x year's time as it is today? Historical information is not always a reliable indicator of future or predictable state, especially during such a rapid upheaval of technology and re-pricing of energy.
I would take as much of the upfront savings as I can now. Plus whatever resale value is anticipated in 5-10 year's time in today's dollars needs to be discounted for future inflation.
[muwu] @Fernet: You're right.
Like most things, the future can't be predicted.
The depreciation curve that EVs have been on, historically, will not be the same in the future. In fact, you can expect them to catch up to hybrids (and ICE) as the cost efficiencies of batteries improve and replacement costs come down.
When that happens, you will see a swing up for EV resales and a swing down for hybrid and certainly ICE resales.
But the future doesn't happen as rapidly as you think. Lithium battery tech has been around for decades, and sure they're taken a giant leap over time, but the refinement takes many years of iterations.
If you have to buy now and assess predictive costs over the medium to long term, you'd have to be overly optimistic that EV battery and depreciation metrics are gonna win out for current 2026 models.
[Fernet] @muwu: Actually I'm more thinking PHEV depreciation will accelerate sooner rather than later. Then it will settle within a niche use case.
And since COVID, this is indeed a period of rapid swings in the used market and resale. Witness diesel passenger cars fall off a cliff in resale value just by themselves.
Sure, it should calm down again. But not for a little while longer.
[muwu] @Fernet: Yep, PHEV are a safer bet on depreciation in the future than full EV.
Still, I've seen the replacement cost of those PHEV batteries and they are steep, really not much less than full EV and certainly not comparable to the lower cost of hybrid batteries. Naturally, the inverse to that cost is the higher entry price and greater depreciation curve of PHEV (but, again, certainly better than full EV).
I'd be more comfortable taking a medium term future bet on a PHEV than a full EV, but it still requires a lot of optimism to think you'll do better on a 2026 model going forward.
[cemenos] If people think about resale value, car is not really the best option for investment. Better you invest on something else let your money sittting there and use the benefit in years from now. (Lets say use deposit with risk and interest rates not inline with inflation means you almost got nothing not worth it the investment)
Buy EV you+partner+family enjoy now daily life with it with style
Financial side
20000km/year for 8 year (for example lifespan of battery warranty)in petrol you will spend $32000 if 100km/8L cosume and petrol only $2.5/L..how much petrol will cost in the future?
Solar can be free using your solar panel to charge your car save that $32000 to cover the depreciation if you want
[maverickjohn] You don't need to change battery after 10 years. I bought a Tesla as they have experience on the road for over 10 years.. how many of those cars have had to replace batteries.. I haven't heard of any. Also Tesla has no regular service intervals like other EVs or ice/hybrid cars which is another saving. I also charge at home for free between 11-2 and so there is another saving.
Honestly having this car has made me wish I did this earlier but better late than never.
[dkausa] Agree. Batteries have proven to be reliable.
Nissan Leafs didn't help the battery reputation. They have no liquid cooling, so really did degrade over time (even in the UK). Many 10-12 year old examples do a max of 80kms of range now with their batteries heading towards 50%-60% state of health.
Most EVs from 2019-on have liquid cooling.Those batteries are lasting well. State of health are still around the 80%-90% mark, and they were higher range with larger KWH batteries as the tech improved.
[muwu] The battery will need replacement. You either take the cost hit as keeping the vehicle and paying for that battery replacement cost, or as depreciation if you sellf before replacement (as the buyer takes on the amortised cost of replacement). Either way, compare that cost with a hybrid, and it is a higher cost, no two ways about it, at least in 2026.
[maverickjohn] Yes the battery will eventually need replacing. But by the time that happens the amount I have saved with all the other savings will still leave me far ahead in comparison to an ice/hybrid.
And maybe by that time the lithiumcarbide cells would be available and we get newer tech battery which is more dense and can go a lot further. But it's more cost effective to go ev than hybrid or ice.
[SBOB] but the EV battery replacement cost is still punitive
Did you include engine replacement cost in your hybrid cost/benefit analysis?
[muwu] I didn't.
Because the internal combustion engine, statistically, with appropriate maintenance, can last an especially long period of car ownership (20-30 years or more). But, yes, the higher maintenance cost of a hybrid ICE engine does need to be taken into account, and thankfully it is less than the 1) higher EV cost, 2) full EV battery replacement cost, 3) EV depreciation.
Those costs will flip once EV battery costs continue to come down.
[Mungulz] I got a BYD Seal Premium for the price of a Camry Ascent hybrid. Even the SL is not specced as well as the seal for $12,000 more.
The Camry is on the TNGA platform dating back to 2018 or so, it’s a lot of money for a car that’s paid off its engineering cost.
Don’t really care about the economics of resale, more concerned about ownership experience, servicing costs, and fuelling costs. If it’s worth $15k less than a Camry Hybrid at end of term, I figure I’m still ahead with lower
running costs and NL savings which wouldn’t apply to an ICE.
I’ll probably buy it out after the lease and keep it for longer though because I’m really happy with it.
[muwu] Don’t really care about the economics of resale, more concerned about ownership experience, servicing costs, and fuelling costs. If it’s worth $15k less than a Camry Hybrid at end of term, I figure I’m still ahead with lower
running costs and NL savings which wouldn’t apply to an ICE.
I mean, I don't mean to be rude, but we are basically on opposite sides of the coin flip here.
I'm the hybrid who has bought at a lower price, has less depreciation, pays for a lower battery replacement (intending to keep long term), and is taking on some higher maintenance costs (for a mass produced Japanese sedan).
You've bought EV and acknowledged, with some degree of cognitive dissonance in the language that you've used, that you will have a greater depreciation curve and/or higher battery replacement cost, amortising away to a greater extent any maintenance or fuelling savings (already low on the comparison with a Japanese manufactured hybrid).
That's true for the economics on 2026. I'm hoping it will be very different in 2036 when I want to be driving an EV too!
[Mungulz] I mean you missed the biggest point, I would have to spend an additional $12,000 to have a worse car. I’m essentially driving a Chinese 5 series or e class for a $48k purchase price.
The resale thing is speculative also, it’s likely to be in the favour of hybrids yes, but potentially in a world where fuel is $5L the EV will be the one to retain value.
[tasbargains] You're more likely to have to replace a mild hybrid battery than a modern EV battery. An LFP pack will outlast the car it is in. There's your (big) mistake.
Plus the tax benefit is huge if you can get it.
[muwu] Tax benefits are much less than depreciation (I've studied it as a healthcare worker with access to some of the most generous FBT benefits).
My hybrid model's batteries have lasted 20 years. I might get less, but it won't be materially different from an EV lifespan, except when it comes to replacement cost (~3-5x less) or associated depreciation if sold prior to replacement needs.
And I intend to keep my hybrid long-term well into its second hybrid battery lifespan, when the amortised costs will be exponentially small.
[littlesoldier] Apart from running cost
the driving experience of EV is much better than petrol car
eg. the acceleration, remote aircon, NFC car key, quietness (no engine noise) etc.
ps: currently owning a BYD EV and a Honda ICE car
[muwu] Agree. What I like most about my hybrid is how it runs on battery, and what I like least is how it runs on an ICE.
However, the economics on the hybrid works. It IS much higher on an EV in 2026. The future will be different, but not quite yet 🙏
[Xizor] Beg to differ on that. Whilst i like certain EVs most have a pretty average to poor driving experience imo. Dont get me wrong far superior comfort, stylish, novel etc sure. 0 to 100 is not nearly as important as handling, ride, feel. A few exceptions of course but its not the majority. Despite looking i still have not found one i like enough to purchase.
[clubhonda] If economic model is the aim buy a used Suzuki Swift. Affordable enough to be 100% cash, simple enough parts to replace and service, and fuel costs are a joke. That's what you should buy id that's really your main criteria.
[muwu] I don't mind spending money. But the value needs to be there, and I don't want to spend more for the same outcome.
I have a large sedan, used model running on a fairly modern platform, hybrid set-up with unbeatable economics, a brand with supreme reliability and low labour and parts costs.
The Suzuki Swift is a worse product for me, where the economics aren't too much better. But buying a new EV, whether it's Tesla or BYD or even a MG or GWM, the economics certainly are a lot worse (in 2026 still) for no better product (except for a preference for a full EV, which is where most EV buyers are but they need to discount their higher costs to justify their decision).
[Legendalvin] The cost of two 8 years throw away EVs equals one 16 years throw away petrol/hybrid car at same tier, Gemini helped me with the math. 20000km per year $2/L fuel and average $0.3/kwh charging.Toyota hybrid even the maintenance cost because of current high purchase price and insurance. For me two separate investments win over one long term investment without putting bet on an ICE car resale value 10 years later.
[muwu] So… are you saying hybrid > EV (in 2026) economically?
[Matt P] I'd argue owning 2 new cars - owned through to 8 years old and "scrapped" (they will have some value - but for Legendalvin's point lets say they don't) has a lot of merit. You're getting a tech/safety upgrade.
The undertone of your posts is that the "Japanese hybrid" which you've still not given any details on, is already used and likely already behind in tech and safety. You have eluded to your car using 4.0l/100 so it must be a Corolla Hybrid/Prius or similar, and to assume from the above posts that the depreciation curve has leveled off, its probably 3-8 years old with 60-140,000kms on the odometer.
When that car was designed, active crash safety has come a long way since. Nobody can change force = mass x acceleration but the car can be smart enough to invervene when you're distracted or haven't noticed that car in your blind spot etc.. In 8 years, those systems will advance significantly. If i look 8 years back, AEB didn't stop for pedestrians/cyclists for most models and blind spot monitoring wasn't commonplace. Your hybrid is already likely a number of years old, add 16 years and it will be prehistoric.
Talk about EV battery replacement/hybrid battery replacement etc.. is completely irrelevant without context on usage. Same on ICE engine wear. My wife's car is a 2 litre turbo which is being destroyed by driving 0.5km-1.7km trips at a time and shut down until its cold again. She could drive my 2023 model EV for likely the next 20 years without battery replacement or even significant battery degradation because of the use case and home charging allowing the battery to be meticulously maintained with slow charging and being kept in the battery chemistrys happy places.
Look, don't get me wrong. You won't catch me dead in a MGS6. Plenty of other fish in the sea though. You can't just unequivocally say JAP HYBRID > EV.
[muwu] @Matt P: The safety conversation is a deep hole to go down.
To keep it short:
Most of the "improvements" in more modern vehicles have been in prevention tech, as you've mentioned examples of. It's the kind of stuff that is eliminating driver behaviour vulnerabilities, rather than making a car grossly safer in a mechanical sense. The latter certainly has improved, mainly through improved crumple zones and air bags, but that is very iterative in a small gradual sense over time.
As a recent driver of an old 90s sedan with little of the more modern preventative tech, my driving behaviour had to compensate. I'm proud to admit how acutely aware I am of road safety and vulnerabilities from my years of experience driving an outdated model. I'm less proud of how that vehicle would have handled a collision if I found myself in that scenario.
Safety is a consideration that lies outside the economic ones. Most commonly, safety is used as a justification to buy a vehicle that is so bad from an economical perspective (especially once minors are included in their family unit). So a consumer will buy that larger SUV, that newer model, and it's justified by considering marginal improvements in safety despite losing $10,000s over their ownership. Then they'll go and drive poorly and demonstrate some pretty maladaptive road behaviour anyway and wipe out any of those marginal safety benefits (doesn't apply to all, but sadly many drivers).
In terms of use case - yeah, your point applies. It's still marginal relative to EV economics. Try applying different use cases to various EVs, with their depreciation / battery replacement costs, and comparing with a hybrid. I know how the math works out on this.
[yummypinacolada] I'm in the same boat as you, despite seeing so many people boasting about how much they've saved by switching to an EV. I'm still using Hybrid by the way, but my next car would def be an EV.
Novated lease: It's probably the cheapest way to get an EV, but I think a lot of people get carried away by the tax savings. For most people, I don't think the actual savings are nearly as big as some claim.
Cheap charging: People often claim they only pay 6–10c per kWh to charge their EVs, but that's a bit misleading. It usually means they're paying higher electricity rates outside off-peak hours. And if they're relying on solar and a battery, they've had to fork out an extra $10k or more upfront.
Low servicing and maintenance costs: This is somewhat true, as long as nothing goes wrong with the car. But when something does go wrong, EVs can often be more expensive to repair.
Despite all that, I still think EVs make a lot of economic sense, depending on how you look at it.
If all you care about is getting from point A to B, buying a used hybrid is probably the cheapest option. But here's where EVs really shine: a sub-$50k EV can already offer loads of high-tech features and a surprisingly luxurious interior and exterior.
You'd never find a comparable ICE car under $50k that offers leather seats, massaging seats, a built-in fridge, a 17-inch screen, advanced ADAS, parking assistance, 360 camera, and so on. I haven't even mention that EV has way more performance than Hybrid or ICE cars.
So I think that's a better way to look at it. With an EV, you're getting a lot more car for your money, rather than necessarily saving a huge amount on running costs. But if your only priority is cheap, reliable commuting, it's hard to beat a used hybrid.
I also don't quite agree that EVs depreciate much quicker than ICE/Hybrid, since the war used EVs have been selling very well. Just have a look at the used Tesla or Byd pricing, they are quite comparable to a hybrid Hyundai, Mazda, or even Toyota.
[muwu] Your analysis is pretty on-point.
To nit pick, you have two biases (which you've acknowledged aren't necessarily economical in your consideration):
The "get-more-for-your-money." It's a modernity factor. Buy a new hybrid (or ICE), and you will get many of the same features. From an engine performance perspective, they differ, like acceleration and noise and energy efficiency. I'm advocating for a used hybrid because of the superior economics, and with an older model comes a loss in those iterative improvements to function (they really are slight year-to-year).
The Iran war reference is very short-termism. I'm not trying to predict future markets (no one can), but long-term averages and mean reversion tends to win out - and it's more than less likely that a resolution to the latest war is struck, fuel prices drift back to a inflationary mean, and the shorter term demand for EV/hybrid levels off. It's not to take away from the longer term trend that we are and will adopt EVs, and 100% so, but it's 2026 and you're assessing the economics this year not for 2036 or 2046.
[yummypinacolada] You generally get more features with EVs compared to their ICE or hybrid counterparts. The Hyundai Kona is a good example, as it's one of the few models available in ICE, hybrid, and EV variants.
If you compare the base models, the EV comes with a lot more features, such as a 12.3-inch multimedia screen, a spare wheel, satellite navigation, rain-sensing wipers, and more (you can compare them yourself on Hyundai's website). None of these features are included in the base ICE or hybrid Kona.
In terms of pricing:
ICE Kona: $37k
Hybrid Kona: $40k
EV Kona: $44k
There's barely any difference in features between the ICE and hybrid variants, so you're essentially paying an extra $3k just for the hybrid powertrain.
With the EV costing only $4k more than the hybrid, I could argue that the $44k EV actually offers better value for money, depending on how much you value those extra features.
Remember EVs generally have much lower running cost, so those extra $4k will slowly even out depending how much you drive.
Like you said, I won't be able to predict how EVs market is going in the future, there's lots of uncertainty. FBT exemption will end soon for EV, so people won't be able to get EV as cheap as now and whether if petrol prices can go back to what it was(or get worse).
[maverickjohn] You are incorrect about the misleading electricity prices. Mine is actually cheaper now than it was prior to EV as ev plans are more favourable
[drprox] I know everyone wants to math this into making sense. We have 2 EVs now. They just drive better. Cost wasn't the key factor in our decision.
[MrZ] Hmm "mid-sze" @ 4700mm length?? Bit of a stretch. More like a large compact.
